Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the final age are generally characterized by conduct that is commonplace and base; yet, those who can transcend evil conditions and pray toward that Pure Land will exhaust their past karmic momentum and be reborn as those of the highest grade.
How much more so when the numinous radiance resides solely within a single hair-tip; how could one who focuses their mind on this profound contemplation fail to transcend birth and death?

At that time, the Bodhisattva, in accordance with their past affinities, expounded the wondrous Dharma for them, causing them to become firm and steadfast, never to regress from the resolve for the unsurpassed path.
The commentary states:
"Afterward" means that [the Bodhisattva] attains it.

By recounting past conditions so as to cause them to remember their former karma, they recognize the cause and know the fruit, thereby naturally achieving non-retrogression; those who were previously non-retrogressive become even more steadfast, and according to their respective stages, they achieve the higher arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
If such sentient beings purify their various karmas and practice these six dharmas, they will, without any doubt, certainly attain rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven and encounter Maitreya.
The commentary states:
Sixth, the summary that concludes the above.
This section has four parts:
First, regarding "attaining birth in the higher realms":
When the three types of karma are all pure and the six matters are practiced in unison, one will be reborn in that heaven; how could this be doubted?
By practicing the six dharmas accordingly and slightly purifying the three karmas, with a mind resolved not to regress, one will certainly be reborn above in the future.
He also followed Maitreya down to Jambudvīpa, where he was the first to hear the Dharma.
The commentary states:
"Second, following [the Buddha] down."
The way of father and son is esteemed for its natural resonance; when the tiger roars and the wind arises, how can one be confused by this?
Those who have fulfilled the six acts and perfected the three karmas, and are reborn in that superior realm, shall hear the Dharma according to the initial assembly.
In future ages, they shall encounter all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
The commentary states:
Third, encountering the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
With wholesome karma fully perfected and right view constantly arising, having already accumulated the provisions of wisdom and merit, he encountered the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Furthermore, during the Nakṣatraprabha kalpa, he also met various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and received the prediction of enlightenment in their presence.
The commentary states:
Fourth, he encountered a Buddha during the Constellation Kalpa.
In the Hinayana, it is said:
In the first eon, one encounters seventy-five thousand Buddhas; in the second eon, seventy-six thousand; and in the third eon, seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.

According to the sixth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, regarding the practice of the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*): in the first reliance, while still on the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), one encounters Buddhas as numerous as five *gaṅgā*-sands;
in the second reliance, from the first through the sixth grounds, one encounters Buddhas as numerous as six *gaṅgā*-sands.
The third reliance is on the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages, where one encounters Buddhas as numerous as the sands of seven Ganges Rivers;
the fourth reliance is on the tenth stage, where one encounters Buddhas as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers.

Bodhisattvas of the first stage encounter one hundred times one hundred billion Buddhas; those of the second stage encounter one thousand times one hundred billion, and so on until the tenth stage, where they encounter immeasurable and boundless numbers.
Therefore, those born there will, by virtue of seeing Maitreya, meet the thousand Buddhas of the Constellation Kalpa (*Tārakā-kalpa*); how could this be doubted?

Regarding the phrase "receiving the prediction of enlightenment" (*bodhisattvavyākaraṇa*), this term applies generally to the preceding context, as the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa also grant such predictions.
There are six types of predictions, as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
The Buddha told Upāli:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if among the great assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, there are those who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and having heard it, feel joy and respectfully prostrate, such persons, at the end of their lives, will attain rebirth in that realm in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, no different from what was described before."
The commentary states:
This second section concerns those who hear the name of the eight classes [of deities] and, with reverence and joy, aspire for rebirth; this constitutes the second of the three grades of birth.
Within it, there are two parts:

The first part clarifies that those who respectfully rejoice and make vows for rebirth [in the Pure Land] will attain it; the latter part clarifies that even those who do not wish for rebirth are benefited by hearing the Name.
This is the former case.

Among the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, those who have previously neither violated the precepts nor committed evil, and whose offenses are slight, will feel joy in their hearts upon hearing the Name. If they then express reverence in speech and perform prostrations with their bodies, although the results will differ according to the superiority or inferiority of their causes, the fact that they receive celestial praise, have their sins eliminated, attain non-retrogression, and encounter a Buddha is no different from what was stated before.

Those who possess all three karmas will be born in the middle-superior grade; those who possess only two karmas will be born in the middle-middle grade; and those who possess only one karma will be born in the middle-inferior grade.

However, even those who merely hear the name of Maitreya will, at the end of their lives, not fall into the dark realms, nor into borderlands, nor into wrong views, nor into any of the evil modes of conduct.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that even hearing the name [of this teaching] brings benefit to those who do not aspire for rebirth.
There are two parts:
There is no evil at the beginning, but there is goodness at the end.
There are four aspects of being without evil:
first, not falling into dark places.
If "dark place" refers to a location in darkness, it denotes the various hells and the intermediate space between the two realms;
if "dark place" refers to a location of dark fruit, it denotes birth within the three evil destinies, the intermediate space between the two realms, or places where the Buddha-dharma does not exist.
Second, not falling into a borderland.
The phrase "not falling" runs through the following three clauses.
What is called a "borderland" refers to various frontier regions that are far removed from the presence of the virtuous and good.
If one practices in a borderland, it is called a "borderland"; this includes regions such as the outlying frontiers, the Mlecchas, and the Daṇḍu, among others.
While the former [refers to] not falling into the three miserable realms, this refers to not falling into the eight unfavorable conditions.
Third, it does not fall into wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
If one were to distinguish wrong view narrowly, it would refer only to the category of severing the roots of goodness;
however, if "wrong" is taken as the definition of wrong view, then all evil views are included.
Fourth, one does not fall into any of the non-virtuous *asaṃvara* (non-restraint).
"Evil" (*pāpa*) means unwholesome; "discipline" (*vinaya*) means dharma; and "observance" (*samiti*) means formality—thus, it refers to non-restraint.

According to the eighth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are fourteen or fifteen types of non-restraint: namely, sheep-slaughterers, poultry-raisers, pig-breeders, bird-catchers, fishers, deer-hunters, rabbit-trappers, robbers, executioners, ox-killers, elephant-binders, those who establish altars to curse dragons, prison guards, slanderers, and those who take pleasure in doing harm, and so forth.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are sixteen [types of killing]; raising oxen, sheep, pigs, and chickens for profit and selling them once they have grown fat constitutes four of these.
For the sake of profit, they purchase [animals] and slaughter them; these constitute four types, which together with the previous [four] make eight.

Fishermen, bird-catchers, hunters, robbers, executioners, those who engage in double-tongued speech, jailers, and dragon-sorcerers—these further constitute eight types, totaling sixteen when combined with the previous ones.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter nine, states that there are twelve [types of livelihood], adding one from the *Abhidharma* and omitting three from the *Abhidharma*.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* also speaks of twelve: namely, sheep-slaughterer, pig-breeder, poultry-keeper, bird-catcher, fisherman, hunter, thief, executioner, prison guard, dragon-charmer, dog-butcher, and ambush-hunter; in total, there are twelve.
Regarding the four differences in textual phrasing: the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* includes three types—those who hunt deer, those who catch rabbits, and those who bind elephants.
The *Abhidharma* (Dharmapada), based on the majority of cases, speaks of only these three; however, the intent of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* extends to include those who catch pheasants and the like.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma* mentions those who delight in causing harm, which is not mentioned in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Because the *Abhidharma* is broad, and because the first eight [chapters] of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* open up distinctions;

that is to say, since the four [factors] arise together according to the *Abhidharma*, the "slander" (*paiśunya*) mentioned in the *Abhidharma* is identical in meaning to "divisive speech" (*piśunavāda*), differing only in name.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and its minor treatises both state that what is grave is called "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*), while the rest, being light, are not.
This non-restraint also encompasses all transgressions of the precepts and evil conduct.
Those who fall into wrong views or improper discipline—whether in a land where a Buddha resides or one where there is no Buddha, whether in a central region or a borderland—all possess these faults.

However, if they hear the name of Maitreya, they will certainly not fall; for their three karmas take refuge [in him], their deep minds rejoice, and the power of his four immeasurable vows adds its majestic influence.
Constantly giving rise to right view, constantly giving rise to the accomplishment of the retinue of right view, and not slandering the Three Jewels.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the presence of virtue.
There are three [factors]:
first, the constant arising of right view, which reverses the aforementioned wrong views;
second, the accomplishment of one's retinue, which reverses the aforementioned failure to undertake the vows of restraint from all unwholesome actions.
Those who possess various evil disciplines do so because of their evil retinues.

The three points regarding not slandering the Triple Gem reverse the previous [conditions]: they do not fall into dark places nor are born in frontier regions, but constantly encounter the Triple Gem and give rise to faith and inclination toward it.
Not only does the middle grade lack the four evil destinies and possess the three good ones, but births corresponding to the upper and lower grades likewise exist.

To clarify that those who hear the Name transform their distinct forms within the eight classes of beings and receive the superior bodies of the four modes of birth, this teaching focuses specifically on the middle grade and elucidates it alone.
The Buddha told Upāli:

"If a son or daughter of good family has violated various prohibitions and committed numerous evil deeds, yet hears the name of this Bodhisattva of Great Compassion and prostrates with their five limbs on the ground, repenting with a sincere heart, all these evil karmas will swiftly become purified."
The commentary states:

This third section concerns the two assemblies who, having committed violations of the precepts, attain purification through repentance and are reborn; this is precisely the third, lowest grade of birth.
Within it, there are three parts:

First, repentance, taking refuge, and the extinction of offenses through practice leading to rebirth; second, attaining non-retrogression upon seeing [the Buddha]; third, encountering a Buddha in the future.
Within the first [section], there are three parts:
first, the extinction of offenses.
There are two ways in which offenses are extinguished:
first, having previously received the precepts and subsequently transgressing them; second, having not previously received the precepts and having committed various evil karmas.

By hearing the name [of the Buddha] and returning with prostration—casting one's five limbs to the ground, including both hands, both feet, and the head—and repenting with utmost sincerity, offenses are swiftly purified.

In future ages, all sentient beings who hear the name of this Bodhisattva’s great compassion shall fashion images of him and offer incense, flowers, robes, silk canopies, banners, and pennants, prostrating before them and maintaining constant mindfulness.
The commentary states:
These two refer to the practice of cultivation.
Even if one does not perform repentance for committed transgressions or make vows for rebirth, but simply cultivates the ten practices, one will certainly attain rebirth there.

First, hearing his name; second, fashioning images of him; third, offering incense; fourth, offering flowers; fifth, offering robes; sixth, offering silk canopies; seventh, offering banners; eighth, offering flags; ninth, constantly prostrating with the body; and tenth, maintaining mindfulness with the mind and speech.

When this person is about to die, Maitreya Bodhisattva will emit from the white tuft between his eyebrows the light of the mark of a great man; together with various devaputras, he will rain down māndārava flowers and come to welcome this person, so that this person shall immediately attain rebirth in that land.
The commentary states:
This is the third rebirth.

Having violated the precepts and committed evil, one repents and returns to purity; by hearing the Name and practicing accordingly, at the moment of death, the Bodhisattva emits the wondrous light from his white tuft of hair to extinguish the darkness of one's transgressions, and rains down the exquisite colors of variegated flowers to nurture the seeds of the Path.
That the Buddhas and devas come to welcome them signifies the profundity of their compassion;
that they attain rebirth in an instant manifests the excellence of their karma.
This section contains three parts:
Those who repent, fashion images, make offerings, prostrate, and maintain constant mindfulness will be reborn in the highest grade of the lower level.
Those who repent, fashion images, make offerings, and prostrate, but do not constantly maintain mindfulness, will be reborn in the middle grade of the lower level.
Those who merely repent, fashion images, and make offerings, but do not constantly prostrate or regularly maintain mindfulness, will be reborn in the lowest grade of the lower level.

Although one may have their transgressions eliminated through returning to repentance, if they do not create images, make offerings, or perform prostrations—whether it be only creating images, only making offerings, only performing prostrations, only maintaining mindful recollection, or even a single invocation of the name—it is still the lowest of the low grade.
It is said that they will not be reborn there, but shall attain liberation within three assemblies.

Encountering Maitreya, they shall prostrate themselves in reverence; before their heads have even been raised, they shall hear the Dharma and immediately attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.
The commentary states:
Second, it is shown that they attain non-retrogression.

When their roots of goodness have long been matured, upon seeing [the Buddha], they immediately pay homage; compassion arises spontaneously within them, and by swiftly hearing the Dharma, they eliminate their lack of faith and quickly attain non-retrogression.
"In future ages, they shall encounter Buddhas, Tathāgatas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The commentary states:
"The third [point] concerns encountering the Buddhas in the future."
The three aforementioned categories clarify the nine grades of rebirth; in all cases, those within the inner assembly personally behold the Buddha and swiftly hear the Dharma.
If one is born among the outer assembly, even at the ninth grade, one will spontaneously attain the stage of non-retrogression at a later time.
The Buddha’s name is Maitreya (the Benevolent One), because he has excellently cultivated himself.
The Buddha told Upāli:
"Listen attentively now."

This Bodhisattva Maitreya shall serve as a great place of refuge for all sentient beings of future ages. If there are those who take refuge in Bodhisattva Maitreya, when he has become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, such practitioners will behold the Buddha’s radiance and immediately receive their prediction of enlightenment.
The commentary states:
The fourth major section generally clarifies that those who possess refuge will not regress and shall attain liberation.
It consists of three parts:
First, clarifying the taking of refuge:

I am the Buddha of True Reward who has already entered parinirvāṇa; as I have not yet encountered disciples of the final dharma age, I entrust all of them to the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya) to deliver.
If one does not see him, one will lose a great benefit; this is called "taking refuge."
Those who take the two refuges shall attain non-retrogression.

Third, when Maitreya attains Buddhahood, those who have attained the noble state will behold the light and receive their prediction [of enlightenment], while ordinary beings will see it as golden in color with their physical eyes.
Tathāgata means "Thus Come One.
Arhat means "Worthy One.
Samyaksaṃbuddha means "Perfectly Enlightened One."
The Buddha told Upāli:

"After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, if any among the fourfold assembly of disciples, or among devas, nāgas, or spirits, should wish to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, they should perform this contemplation and fix their mindfulness upon it."
The commentary states:

The fifth major section clarifies the extent to which those of the upper nine grades who aspire for rebirth eliminate their transgressions by practicing the ten virtuous deeds, reciting the Name, and maintaining reverence, etc.
Within this, there are two parts:
The first section clarifies birth through pleasure, where birth is attained when karma is fulfilled;
the latter section clarifies non-pleasure, where even the practice has not yet been fulfilled.
Within the birth through pleasure, there are four types:
First, to cause mindfulness; second, to encourage practice; third, to teach aspiration; fourth, to extinguish transgressions.
This is the first [point].

One should mindfully recollect Tuṣita Heaven, uphold the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts for one day up to seven days, and contemplate the ten wholesome actions while practicing the path of the ten wholesome deeds.
The commentary states:
This is the second exhortation to practice.

For now, we shall discuss the observance of the precepts alone, setting aside other deeds; even the most minimal duration—from one day to seven days—can lead to rebirth in the Pure Land, let alone those who have practiced for many years and many lifetimes.
Since all virtues are fully encompassed within the ten wholesome paths, one should reflect upon them.
When the practice is based on these weighty principles, it is called the "ten wholesome paths.
With this merit, when dedicating it with the aspiration to be born before Maitreya, one should perform this visualization.
The commentary states:
This is the third teaching on vows.
If one practices without vows, that practice will inevitably be solitary; it may not necessarily lead to rebirth in the realm of Maitreya.

If there is aspiration without practice, that aspiration will surely be empty; since there was no prior cause, the fruit cannot arise. Therefore, the teaching is that aspiration and practice must support one another.

For one who practices this contemplation, whether they see a single celestial being seated upon a lotus flower, or for even a single moment of thought they invoke the name of Maitreya, such a person shall eliminate the karmic offenses of birth and death accumulated over twelve hundred kalpas.
The commentary states:
The fourth section concerns the eradication of sins.
It consists of three parts:
First, fixing one's thoughts upon encountering the conditions; second, giving rise to reverence upon hearing the name; third, prostrating with total sincerity.
This refers to the first. Regarding the first condition, there are two types:
There are two [objects of focus]: first, sentient beings; second, all phenomena.

Regarding the observation of a single celestial being or human: whenever one encounters the conditions of a single sentient being, one should immediately bring Maitreya to mind—contemplating how to uproot their suffering, provide them with joy, eliminate their evils, and embrace their virtues; admiring those who are superior, feeling aversion toward those who are inferior; honoring virtuous friends and rejecting evil associates.

Upon seeing a single lotus flower, one should immediately bring to mind Maitreya according to whatever dharma is encountered: regarding a favorable dharma, one should think of making offerings; regarding an unfavorable dharma, one should think of not encountering it again; regarding defiled dharmas, one should rejoice in their abandonment; and regarding pure dharmas, one should rejoice in their cultivation.

In this context, taking sentient beings and a single phenomenon as examples, one contemplates Maitreya; this intention generally reveals the practice of performing the karma for rebirth in the upper realms.
Those who cultivate these two categories should reflect upon him whenever conditions arise, contemplating him at all times without even a moment’s interruption or abandonment.

If one contemplates for even a single moment, the sins of birth and death accumulated over twelve hundred kalpas will be extinguished; this is because Maitreya’s past vows and the practitioner’s single-minded devotion have brought about this result.

Amitābha Buddha entered parinirvāṇa eighty kalpas ago, whereas Maitreya’s former vow-power was different; because their depth of compassion and the nature of their lands—joyful or suffering—are distinct, there is a difference in the weight of their devotees’ joyful aspiration, as explained in the previous comparative analysis.
If one merely hears the name of Maitreya and joins their palms in reverent worship, this person shall eliminate the karmic offenses of fifty kalpas of birth and death.
The commentary states:
"The second [case] is hearing the name and giving rise to reverence."
The previous explanation stated that if one encounters the conditions for a single thought-moment, one extinguishes twelve hundred kalpas of afflictions;
this refers merely to hearing the name, joining one's palms, and paying respectful homage, which removes fifty kalpas.
If one merely initiates the physical act of prostration but the head does not reach the ground, it is because the mind lacks sincerity.
However, for those who pay respectful homage to Maitreya, the sins of birth and death accumulated over ten billion kalpas shall be eliminated.
The commentary states:
Third is prostration with total devotion.

By touching one’s head to the ground, continuing day and night, one eliminates the sins of ten billion kalpas; this is because both the physical body and the mind are equally surrendered, and both are treated with equal gravity.

This is the most grave; seeing the hair-tuft is the second; for a single moment [of thought] is the third; hearing the name and joining one’s palms is the fourth, because their gravity and lightness differ.
Question:
Why is seeing the hair-tuft on the body not as [meritorious] as recollecting it from afar?
Answer:

Seeing the physical marks of the Buddha’s body truly eliminates much more demerit. This is because practicing while contemplating him from afar is difficult to bring about, whereas taking refuge and paying homage upon seeing him is easy to initiate.
Regarding the method of transformative teaching, one first exhorts others to perform what is difficult to cultivate, and subsequently exhorts them to perform what is easy to practice.

Furthermore, because the suffering of humans is heavy, their inclination toward joy is exceptionally deep; whereas because the pleasures of the heavens are abundant, their sense of weariness is truly shallow.
Moreover, for one who contemplates from afar, even a single thought-moment is long in duration because it is a mental construction.

Those who see the light do so for only a brief moment; because this duration is short and it is seen with the eyes, those who remember [the Buddha] from afar eliminate more demerit, whereas those who see the light of the ūrṇā-kośa eliminate less demerit.
Question:
It is clearly stated in minor sutras that hearing the name and recollecting it with devotion eradicates much demerit.
How much merit is there in creating an image for worship?
Answer: The merit is even greater because the activity is continuous and the mindfulness is also great.

Herein, I have merely cited the case of a brief hearing upon a single momentary return and prostration; if one hears [the teaching] repeatedly, pays homage frequently, and makes offerings every morning, the merit is even greater.
In the first three chapters, the cultivation [of refuge] merely clarifies the merit of attaining birth [in higher realms], without yet discussing the characteristics of the destruction of sins;
in the second section, it clarifies the benefits of non-retrogression through taking refuge;

now, in this third section, it finally clarifies the destruction of sins, which is to say, it provides a general exposition on performing the Great Refuge, causing sentient beings to joyfully give rise to devotion and thereby destroy their sins.
Even if one does not take birth in the heavens, in a future age one shall likewise encounter [the Buddha] beneath the Dragon-Flower Bodhi tree and resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the lack of delight in rebirth.
Those whose karmic forces were not yet full also gave rise to the aspiration for the Way during the three assemblies at the Dragon Flower Tree.
Those who had previously sought rebirth in the heavens, having fulfilled the three grades of karma, attained the Way at all three assemblies at the Dragon Flower Tree;
these [others] merely gave rise to the aspiration, and thus there is a distinction between them.
The second fascicle of the *Bodhisattvagatyutpatti-sūtra* states: "Your birth in a land of happiness is not like my land of suffering.
Your preaching of the Dharma is very easy; my preaching of the Dharma is very difficult."
First, ninety-six were mentioned who received my five precepts;
next, ninety-four were mentioned who upheld the three refuges;
finally, ninety-two were mentioned who uttered "Namo Buddha" but once.
According to the actual fact, those born in the superior grade practice the six matters of the Dharma.
That sutra merely states that they receive my five precepts.

As for those delivered in the first assembly, they only carry out one of the six matters; this is because their majestic deportment is complete and they are subsumed under the single matter of the superior grade.

Those who receive and uphold the Three Refuges and are delivered in the second assembly are born into the middle-three grades, specifically the middle-middle and middle-superior grades, because they possess the three types of karma.

Those who recite "Namo Buddha" once and are delivered in the third assembly are subsumed within the lower-three grades, specifically the lower-lower grade, because they merely recite it with their mouths.
That sutra merely cites one example from each of the three categories; as it is intended for coarse, conventional practice and does not provide a complete exposition, there is no contradiction.

When these words were spoken, an immeasurable multitude rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, prostrated at Maitreya’s feet, and circumambulated the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Maitreya hundreds of thousands of times.
The commentary states:
This concludes the second major section from below, which encourages birth therein and involves the arousal of rare aspirations by the multitude.
It consists of two parts:
First, the assembly makes rare vows; later, the Buddha grants the prediction of their rebirth.
Within the vows, there are two parts:
first, clarifying their dignified demeanor; second, clarifying the making of the vows.
This is the first [point].
"Rising from his seat" signifies being born there, arising from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
"Prostrating at the two feet" signifies the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Circumambulating the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas one hundred thousand times signifies that throughout a hundred thousand lifetimes they shall never be separated from them.
Those who had not yet attained the Way each made a vow:

"We, the eight classes of devas and humans, now before the Buddha make this sincere vow: may we, in future lives, encounter Maitreya; and after casting off these bodies, may we all attain rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven."
The commentary states:
This is the formulation of a vow.
Those who have not yet attained the Way are referred to merely as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), because the sages follow their vows.
Non-returners, those beyond training, and others may travel by means of supernatural powers.
To encourage and exhort those of the final age, I have mentioned only ordinary beings and not spoken of the passage of sages.
In the future, they shall encounter the three assemblies and attain liberation; only after casting off this body do they aspire to be born in the higher realms.
The World-Honored One declared:
"You and those who in future ages cultivate merit and uphold the precepts shall all be reborn before Maitreya Bodhisattva and be received into his care."
The commentary states:
This concludes the Buddha’s prediction of rebirth.

You and all future practitioners of inferior capacity who, even for a single thought-moment, invoke the name of Maitreya, shall all attain birth there; how much more so those of superior capacity who are able to cultivate merit and uphold the precepts? How could they not be born there?
Because those of the three vehicles and the five vehicles are all delivered and liberated by it, the Buddha told Upāli:
"One who practices this contemplation is said to practice correctly; one who contemplates otherwise is said to practice erroneously."
The commentary states:
This third major section on exhorting rebirth therein concludes the correct contemplation.
Out of compassion for those in the final age, it earnestly exhorts one to go there.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How excellent!"

The World-Honored One has eloquently expounded all the merits of Maitreya and has also prophesied the karmic rewards to be obtained by sentient beings who cultivate merit in the future; I now rejoice in this.
The commentary states:
This is the third major section within the entire work, titled "The Section on Rejoicing upon Hearing the Name and Practicing with Joy."
Within this, there are four sections:
first, the question; second, the answer; third, the benefits obtained by the assembly at that time; and fourth, the joyful departure and circulation [of the teaching].
In the first [section], there are two parts: [End of provided text]
First, there is the praise and exposition of sympathetic joy; subsequently, there is the formal inquiry regarding the holding of the name.
This is the former [section].
Because it extols the meritorious deeds and their fruits for both ordinary beings and sages, the preceding discourse establishes that all [merit] pertains to both types of karmic response.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
How should this essential Dharma be received and upheld?"
"What should this sutra be named?
The commentary says:
This question concerns the retention of the name.
"Veyan" (So be it) is a term of respectful assent.
How should this essential and subtle sūtra be received and upheld?
Furthermore, what is the name of the ritual procedure for its practice?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Uphold these words of the Buddha; be careful not to forget or lose them.
For the sake of future generations, open the path to rebirth in the heavens, reveal the signs of Bodhi, and do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas."
The commentary states:
The second section is the sequential response.
It is divided into two parts:
This is the response regarding upholding [the teaching].

Now that I am entering parinirvāṇa, beings of the final age will be without reliance; therefore, I exhort you to uphold [this] and command that it not be treated with negligence. This is so that, in the future, they may near-attain the bliss of the Dharma within the heavens and abandon the ruinous sinking into the four realms of existence, while far manifesting the wondrous marks of Bodhi, emerging from the triple world and soaring beyond it.
The Sūtras state that when one has well-established roots of goodness, the extinction of the Dharma severs the lineage of the Buddha.
The Buddha refers to Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-vijñāna), and "lineage" is termed the causal wisdom.
Wisdom arises through study; without study, the lineage is severed.

This sutra is titled "The Parinirvāṇa of Maitreya Bodhisattva," and it is also titled "Contemplating Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven and Exhorting One to Generate the Bodhicitta"; thus should it be upheld.
The commentary states:
This is the direct answer regarding the title.
It is so titled because it explains the matter of the parinirvāṇa of Maitreya Bodhisattva.
By manifesting the appearance of birth therein, it inspires contemplation; it exhorts the arousal of the bodhicitta so that it may circulate through ten thousand generations.
To explain the meaning according to the names, one should maintain them in this way:
"receiving" (śīla) means taking [the precepts] into one's heart, and "maintaining" (dhāraṇa) means upholding them without falsehood.
When the Buddha spoke these words, one hundred thousand bodhisattvas who had gathered from other directions attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
The commentary states:
"The assembly of the third period obtained benefit."
There are two [benefits]:
first, the benefit for the noble ones; second, the benefit for ordinary beings.
This is the former.
Eighty trillion devas resolved their minds on Bodhi, all vowing to follow Maitreya in his descent to be born in this world.
The commentary states:
"This is the benefit for ordinary beings."
"Not only did they resolve their minds at that time, but they also vowed to descend in the future.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the fourfold assembly, the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy; they prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
The commentary states:
The fourth [chapter], "Joy," concerns the circulation [of the teaching].
Having attained what was never before attained, one rejoices because of this.
Having completed the task according to the instructions, I now withdraw this for circulation.
In the final age of the world, evil fruits arise from evil causes; one may find oneself before or after a Buddha, dwelling long within the states of no leisure.
If one aspires to birth in the Pure Land, wondrous practices will not be perfected;
if one hopes for the celestial palaces, it is feared that the superior causes will not be cultivated.
Although the Pure Land is free from defilement, the holy teachings themselves naturally contain variations.
Although there are sensual pleasures within the celestial palaces, this principle is certain and free from doubt.
For one who is weary of sensory objects, they are defiled by contact with things yet remain undefiled;
for one who is addicted to sensual pleasures, they are undefiled by these very things yet remain defiled.

When the karma of precepts is deficient and merit and wisdom are shallow, the Buddha manifests in a defiled realm in response to the capacities of sentient beings; likewise, ordinary beings rejoice in birth by acceding to the realm of the Sage.
Since even the supreme sages and the most eminent worthies engaged in this very karma, how could those of lower station among the common folk transcend it?
Therefore, those whose practices are identical should all cultivate them with single-minded devotion.
Guided by my own insights, I hope these may serve as causes for future lives;
as for other details regarding his conduct and traces, they are fully recorded in separate biographies.

The fourth fascicle of the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) of the Great Song states: "Later, he traveled in person to Mount Wutai; ascending to Daxing and proceeding to Xihe, he stayed overnight in an ancient Buddhist temple."
In his dream, he was at the foot of a mountain crag where immeasurable people were crying out in suffering.
Amidst the darkness and obscurity, he could not initially bear to hear them.
He ascended those tiered peaks on foot; they were all the color of lapis lazuli, and he beheld all the various lands within them.
Looking up at the city, a voice from within it cried out: "Stop!
Stop! Ho!"
"Master Ji has not yet ordered me to come here.
After a short while, two celestial youths emerged from the city and asked,
"Do you see the sentient beings suffering in the hells beneath the mountain?"
He replied, "I heard the sound, but I did not see the form.
The youth then threw him a sword hilt and said:
"I shall see [the truth] by cutting open my own belly.
Daoki cut it himself; as his abdomen opened, two streams of light shone forth, illuminating the foot of the mountain, where he saw countless people undergoing extreme suffering.
At that time, the youth entered the city and offered two scrolls of paper and a brush; [the monk] received them with both hands and departed.
When dawn arrived, his astonishment was still not over, for he saw a light within the Guoxin Temple that did not extinguish for a long time.

Upon searching through them, he found that several scrolls emitted light; when he examined them, he discovered the *Maitreya’s Ascent to Heaven Sūtra*. He then recalled his previous dream, realizing it must have been Maitreya who had commanded him to compose a commentary to clarify its principles.
Thereupon, as he cast his brush into the inkwell, twenty-seven śarīra relics fell from the tip of the pen; they were about the size of Chinese *hántáo* cherries and a lovely red color.
Following these, others fell in a scattered manner, resembling grains of yellow millet or *liáng* millet, so it is said.
Relying on this, I have praised the attainment of the meaning; I shall now expound and lecture upon the original sutra.
Rejoicing in this gift of Dharma, I proceed in due order to the capital;
There, the Compassionate Honored One receives me with instruction, Revealing that the Dharmakāya is without marks.
The End of the Praise for the Sutra on the Visualization of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven, Volume II.
